g-c1-1.s: King Gylfi ruled the land that is now called Sweden. It is said that he gave a travelling woman, as a reward for entertaining him, a piece of ploughland in his kingdom: as much as four oxen could plough in a day and a night. But this woman was of the family of the Æsir; her name was Gefjun. From Jötunheim in the north she brought four oxen, her sons by a giant, and harnessed them to the plough. The plough cut so wide and so deep that it tore the land loose, and the oxen dragged it out to sea, westwards, until they stopped in a certain strait. There Gefjun set the land down and named it Selund. Ever since, the place where the land was torn away has been water: it is now called the Lögr, in Sweden, and the bays of that lake match the headlands of Selund. As Bragi, the poet of old, says:

l: Gefjun gladly dragged from Gylfi | the wave-wealth's freehold,
to Denmark's gain, | while the running beasts steamed with sweat;
the oxen carried, besides, | eight eyes, bright brow-lamps,
and four heads as they hauled | the broad plunder of the field.

g-c2-1.s: King Gylfi was a wise man and skilled in magic. It troubled him greatly that the Æsir were so clever that everything went as they wished. He wondered whether this came from their own nature, or whether the gods they worshipped made it so. He set out for Ásgard in secret, disguised as an old man. But the Æsir were wiser: they had second sight, saw him coming long before he arrived, and prepared illusions to deceive his eyes. When he came into the stronghold he saw a hall so high that he could hardly make out the top of it. Its roof was laid with golden shields, like shingles. As Thjódólfr of Hvin also says, Valhall was roofed with shields:

l: On their backs they let shine, | badly battered by stones,
the shingles of Odin's hall, | those shrewd seafarers.

g-c2-3.s: In the doorway of the hall Gylfi saw a man juggling with short swords, keeping seven in the air at once. The man asked his name. He said he was called Gangleri, that he had come a long and winding way, and asked for a bed for the night. "Who owns this hall?" he asked.

g-c2-4.s: The man replied that it belonged to their king. "I will take you to him," he said, "and then you can ask him his name yourself." He turned and led the way into the hall; Gylfi followed, and at once the door closed behind him.

g-c2-5.s: Inside he saw a great room full of people: some were playing games, some were drinking, and some were armed and fighting. He looked around and found much of what he saw hard to believe, and he said:

l: Every doorway, | before you go out,
you should scan:
for you cannot know | where enemies sit
on the benches ahead.

g-c2-7.s: He saw three high seats, one above another, and a man sat on each. He asked what the names of these lords were.

g-c2-8.s: The man who had brought him in answered that the one on the lowest high seat was a king, "and his name is Hárr; the next is called Jafnhárr; and the one at the top is called Thridi."

g-c2-9.s: Then Hárr asked the newcomer whether he had come for anything more than food and drink, which were always his for the asking, as for everyone in the High One's hall. Gangleri said that first he wanted to find out whether there was any wise man inside.

g-c2-10.s: Hárr said that he would not leave unharmed unless he proved the wiser:

l: Step forward, | you who ask;
the one who answers | shall sit.

g-c3-1.s: Gangleri began his questions like this: "Who is the highest, or the oldest, of all the gods?"

g-c3-2.s: Hárr answered: "In our language he is called Allfather, but in the old Ásgard he had twelve names. The first is Allfather; the second Lord, or Lord of Hosts; the third Nikarr, or Spear-Lord; the fourth Nikudr, or Striker; the fifth Knower of Many Things; the sixth Granter of Wishes; the seventh Far-Speaker; the eighth Shaker, or the One Who Puts Armies to Flight; the ninth Burner; the tenth Destroyer; the eleventh Protector; the twelfth Gelding."

g-c3-3.s: Then Gangleri asked: "Where is this god? What power does he have, and what great deeds has he done?"

g-c3-4.s: Hárr answered: "He lives through all ages, rules his whole kingdom and governs all things, great and small."

g-c3-5.s: Then Jafnhárr said: "He made heaven and earth and the air, and everything in them."

g-c3-6.s: Then Thridi said: "Greatest of all, he made man and gave him a spirit that will live and never die, even when the body rots to dust or burns to ashes. All who live rightly will live on and be with him in the place called Gimlé. But the wicked go to Hel, and from there down to the Misty Hel, which lies below in the ninth world."

g-c3-7.s: Then Gangleri said: "What was he doing before heaven and earth were made?"

g-c3-8.s: Hárr answered: "Then he was with the frost giants."

g-c4-1.s: Gangleri said: "What was the beginning? How did things begin, and what was there before?"

l: It was the dawn of time, | when nothing was:
no sand, no sea, | no cool waves;
there was no earth, | no heaven above,
only a yawning gap, | and no grass anywhere."

g-c4-4.s: Then Jafnhárr said: "Many ages before the earth was made, the World of Mist was made. In the middle of it lies the spring called Hvergelmir, and from it flow the rivers called Svöl, Gunnthrá, Fjörm, Fimbulthul, Slídr and Hríd, Sylgr and Ylgr, Víd and Leiptr; Gjöll flows close to the gates of Hel." And Thridi said: "But first of all there was the world in the south called Múspell. It is bright and hot; that region blazes and burns, and no one who is a stranger there and has no home in it can pass through.

g-c4-5.s: The one who sits at the edge of that land to defend it is called Surtr. He wields a flaming sword, and at the end of the world he will come out and make war, defeat all the gods and burn the whole world with fire. As it says in Völuspá:

l: Surtr comes from the south | with the flame that devours branches;
from his sword shines | the sun of the gods of war.
Rocky cliffs crash, | the fiends stagger,
men tread the road to Hel, | and heaven splits apart."

g-c5-1.s: Gangleri asked: "How were things arranged before there were families, and before the human race multiplied?"

g-c5-2.s: Then Hárr said: "The rivers called the Ice-waves had flowed so far from their source that the poisonous yeast in them hardened like the slag that runs from a furnace, and turned to ice. When the ice stopped and no longer flowed, it froze over on top. The drizzle that rose from the poison froze into rime, and the rime built up, layer upon layer, all the way into Ginnungagap, the Yawning Void."

g-c5-3.s: Then Jafnhárr said: "The northern part of Ginnungagap filled with heavy masses of ice and rime, and within it drizzle and gusts of wind; but the southern part of the Yawning Void was lit by the sparks and glowing embers that flew out of Múspellheim."

g-c5-4.s: And Thridi said: "Just as cold and everything harsh came out of Niflheim, so everything facing Múspellheim was hot and bright. But Ginnungagap was as mild as still air. When the warm breath met the rime, so that it melted and dripped, life sprang from the drops of yeast, through the power of the one who sent the heat, and took the shape of a man. He is called Ymir, but the frost giants call him Aurgelmir, and from him come the families of the frost giants, as it says in The Shorter Völuspá:

l: All the witches | come from Witolf,
all the wizards | from Willharm,
and the spell-singers | from Swarthead;
all the giants | come from Ymir.

g-c5-6.s: And about this the giant Vafthrúdnir says:

l: Out of the Ice-waves | spattered drops of poison,
growing until | a giant was made;
from him all our kin | are descended,
and that is why | we are always so fierce."

g-c5-8.s: Then Gangleri said: "How did the families grow from there? How did it come about that there were more people?

g-c5-9.s: Or do you take him for a god, the one you just spoke of?" And Jafnhárr answered: "We certainly do not regard him as a god. He was evil, and so were all his descendants: we call them frost giants. It is said that while he slept he broke into a sweat, and under his left arm grew a man and a woman, and one of his legs fathered a son with the other. That is where the families come from: these are the frost giants. The old frost giant we call Ymir."

g-c6-1.s: Then Gangleri said: "Where did Ymir live, and what did he live on?"

g-c6-2.s: Hárr answered: "As soon as the rime dripped, a cow called Audumla came into being from it. Four rivers of milk flowed from her udders, and she fed Ymir."

g-c6-3.s: Then Gangleri asked: "And what did the cow feed on?"

g-c6-4.s: "She licked the blocks of ice, which were salty. On the first day she licked them, a man's hair came out of the ice by evening; on the second day, a man's head; on the third day the whole man was there. His name was Búri. He was handsome, big and strong. He had a son called Borr, who married a woman called Bestla, the daughter of the giant Bölthorn, and they had three sons: the first was Odin, the second Vili, the third Vé. And I believe that this Odin and his brothers must be the rulers of heaven and earth. We think that is what he should be called: that is the name of the one we know to be the greatest and most worthy of honour, and you would do well to call him so too."

g-c7-1.s: Then Gangleri said: "How did they get on together, and which side was the stronger?"

g-c7-2.s: Hárr answered: "The sons of Borr killed the giant Ymir. When he fell, so much blood poured from his wounds that it drowned the whole race of frost giants, except one, whom the giants call Bergelmir, who escaped with his household. He climbed onto his ship with his wife, and they were saved. From them come the families of the frost giants, as it says here:

l: Countless ages | before the earth was made,
Bergelmir was born;
the first thing I remember | is how that famous wise giant
was laid on the deck of a ship."

g-c8-1.s: Then Gangleri said: "What did the sons of Borr do next, if you believe they are gods?"

g-c8-2.s: Hárr replied: "There is a great deal to tell about that. They took Ymir, carried him into the middle of the Yawning Void and made the earth out of him: the sea and the lakes from his blood, the land from his flesh, the cliffs from his bones; and from his teeth, his molars and the bones that were broken they made rocks and stones."

g-c8-3.s: And Jafnhárr said: "From the blood that flowed freely from his wounds they made the sea, once they had shaped the earth and made it firm, and they laid the sea in a ring around it. Most people would find it hard to cross."

g-c8-4.s: Then Thridi said: "They also took his skull and made the sky from it, and raised it over the earth with four corners, and under each corner they placed a dwarf. Their names are East, West, North and South. Then they took the glowing embers and sparks that had shot out of Múspellheim and set them in the middle of the Yawning Void, in the sky above and below, to light heaven and earth. They gave every fire its place: some were fixed in the sky, others wandered freely beneath it, but these too were given places and set on their courses. Old poems say that from them the days were counted and the years reckoned, as it says in Völuspá:

l: The sun did not know | where her home was;
the moon did not know | what power he had;
the stars did not know | where their places were.
So it was before | the earth was made."

g-c8-7.s: Then Gangleri said: "This is great news to hear; that is a marvellous piece of work, and skilfully made.

g-c8-8.s: How was the earth arranged?" And Hárr answered: "It is round on the outside, and around it lies the deep sea. Along the shore of that sea they gave land to the families of giants to live in. But further in, they built a stronghold around the world against the hostility of the giants, and for its wall they used the eyebrows of the giant Ymir. They called that place Midgard. They also took his brain, threw it into the air and made the clouds from it, as it says here:

l: From Ymir's flesh | the earth was made,
and from his sweat the sea;
cliffs from his bones, | trees from his hair,
and from his skull the sky.
Then from his eyebrows | the kindly gods
made Midgard for the sons of men;
and from his brain | all the gloomy
clouds were made."

g-c9-1.s: Then Gangleri said: "They had certainly achieved a great deal, it seems to me, when earth and heaven were made, the sun and the stars set in place and the days divided. But where do the people who live in the world come from?"

g-c9-2.s: Hárr answered: "As the sons of Borr were walking along the seashore, they found two trees. They picked them up and made people from them. The first gave them spirit and life; the second, understanding and feeling; the third, appearance, speech, hearing and sight. They gave them clothes and names: the man was called Askr and the woman Embla, and from them came the human race, which was given a home inside Midgard. Next they built themselves a city in the middle of the world, called Ásgard; people call it Troy. There the gods and their families lived, and many events and stories have come from there, both on earth and in the sky. There is a place called Hlidskjálf, and when Allfather sat in the high seat there, he could see over the whole world and everything everyone did, and he understood all that he saw. His wife was called Frigg, the daughter of Fjörgvinn, and from them comes the family we call the Æsir, who settled the old Ásgard and the kingdoms that belong to it; and that is a race of gods. That is why he is called Allfather: he is the father of all the gods and of people, and of everything that he and his power brought about. The Earth was his daughter and his wife; with her he had his first son, Ása-Thor. Strength and might go with him, and with them he overcomes every living thing.

g-c10-1.s: "Nörfi or Narfi was the name of a giant who lived in Jötunheim. He had a daughter called Night, who was dark and swarthy, like all her family. She was married to a man called Naglfari, and their son was Audr. After that she married a man called Annarr, and their daughter was Jörd. Last of all Dayspring married her, and he was of the family of the Æsir; their son was Day, who was bright and beautiful like his father. Then Allfather took Night and her son Day, gave them two horses and two chariots, and set them up in the sky to ride around the earth, each in turn, once every day and night. Night rides first, on the horse called Frosty-Mane, and every morning he wets the earth with the foam from his bit. Day's horse is called Sheen-Mane, and his mane lights up all the sky and the earth."
